title: Waiting for Big Mo

jokes.text: Charlie trying to fit all five toes into five-finger shoes, unable to locate his pinky toe
jokes.setup: Dennis asks what Charlie is doing
jokes.punchline: Charlie is struggling to identify which toe is his pinky in order to fit it into the correct slot of five-finger shoes
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie opening — his obliviousness and incompetence with mundane tasks is core character comedy. The image of a grown man unable to identify his own pinky toe is absurd and perfectly Charlie-coded. Good character integration.

dialogue.line: Charlie struggling to put his toes in five-fingered shoes, can't tell where his pinky is

jokes.text: Charlie's reason for getting five-finger shoes: so he can still effectively be barefoot while technically wearing shoes, in response to Dennis yelling at him for taking his shoes off during laser tag
jokes.setup: Dennis asks why Charlie got the stupid five-finger shoes
jokes.punchline: Charlie's logic: Dennis yells at him for removing shoes, so he found shoes that are basically bare feet — solving the problem while missing the entire point
jokes.explanation: This is a great Charlie joke because his logic is internally coherent but completely misses the point. He heard 'wear shoes' and found the most literal loophole possible. Strong character integration — this could only be Charlie. The setup/payoff structure is tight and the absurd reasoning lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got five-finger shoes because Dennis yells at me for taking my shoes off in laser tag, and I wanted shoes that were more like bare feet

jokes.text: Dennis explains he yells at Charlie about shoes because without shoes Charlie isn't holding his gun — and because the cheese oozes out of his feet
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the practical reason for yelling at Charlie about shoes (not holding gun)
jokes.punchline: He adds a second reason: the cheese Charlie hides in his shoes oozes out and smells awful
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie hides cheese in his shoes is delivered as a throwaway second reason, which makes it funnier. It's deeply Charlie-specific gross-out humor that is completely normalized within the show's world — classic IASIP structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie takes shoes off, doesn't hold gun, plus cheese oozes out of his feet with awful smell

jokes.text: "That's the cheese I hide in my shoes, that's where it is." — Charlie confirms, undisturbed, that yes, he does hide cheese in his shoes
jokes.setup: Dennis reveals the cheese oozes out of Charlie's feet
jokes.punchline: Charlie confirms the cheese-in-shoes habit without a hint of shame, as if this is completely normal and his only concern is shoe accessibility
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie delivery. The joke isn't that he hides cheese in his shoes — it's that this is so normal to him that his only complaint about the five-finger shoes is that he can't store cheese in them anymore. The economy is excellent; it's a one-liner that reveals an entire worldview. High quotability for Always Sunny fans.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I hide cheese in my shoes, okay? But I can't fit cheese in the five-finger shoes.

jokes.text: "I can't even, like, fit cheese in these shoes. These things suck."
jokes.setup: Charlie has been complaining about five-finger shoes being hard to wear
jokes.punchline: His final verdict on the shoes is not about comfort or function — it's that he can't hide cheese in them
jokes.explanation: This is the button on the cheese-in-shoes bit. The economy is superb — it's Charlie's entire character in one sentence. Excellent callback that closes the shoe bit perfectly while reinforcing the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm kind of sick and tired of guarding the base. I want to go out there and have some fun.

jokes.text: "Some people might think that's sad, but that's not sad. That's cool." — Dennis and Charlie reassuring each other that playing laser tag for a very long time is cool, not sad
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how long they've been playing laser tag; they both agree it's been a long time
jokes.punchline: Both immediately and defensively insist this is cool, not sad — the defensiveness itself confirming it's sad
jokes.explanation: This is also the episode's first meta-layer joke — the characters are defending the premise of the whole show (terrible people doing the same thing forever). The irony that reassuring yourself something isn't sad confirms it is sad works well here.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why do blind people hate skydiving? Because it scares the hell out of their dogs

jokes.text: "Why do blind people hate skydiving? 'Cause it scares the hell out of their dogs."
jokes.setup: Charlie proposes doing riddles to pass time; Dennis reluctantly asks why blind people hate skydiving
jokes.punchline: Because it scares the hell out of their dogs — referring to guide dogs, a non-sequitur punchline
jokes.explanation: A passable joke that works mainly because Charlie insists it's a riddle. The punchline is weak but the framing and ensuing argument about whether it's a joke or riddle is where the comedy is generated.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: 'That's not a riddle'

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Yeah, it's a riddle about blind people and their dogs'

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: 'That's a joke'

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Jokes are funny and that wasn't funny'

jokes.text: The argument about whether the blind skydiving thing is a joke or a riddle — "Jokes are funny and that wasn't funny." "I didn't say it was funny." "Then how is it a joke, Dennis?"
jokes.setup: Dennis says the blind skydiving thing is a joke, not a riddle
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out jokes are supposed to be funny, it wasn't funny, so by Dennis's own logic it isn't a joke — accidentally valid philosophical point
jokes.explanation: Charlie accidentally wins a logic argument with Dennis, which is funny on its own. The structure is tight — Charlie's dim literalism produces an accidentally airtight philosophical point that Dennis can't counter. This is the show at its best when Charlie's obliviousness accidentally cuts through.

dialogue.line: Mac and Dee tumbling out of air ducts, fighting and covered in dust

jokes.text: Mac and Dee crashing out of the air ducts having gotten tangled up — with Dee having spit in Mac's mouth after he elbowed her in the tit
jokes.setup: Dennis had Mac and Dee in the air ducts sniping opposing bases
jokes.punchline: They collided in the ducts, got tangled, and Dee spit in Mac's mouth in retaliation for being elbowed in the breast
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP physical escalation — the indignity of crawling through ducts compounded by getting spat on. The visual of two adults tumbling out of ceiling ducts is inherently funny and sets up the insult exchange to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I spit in your mouth after you jammed me in the tit with your scrawny little elbow

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My elbows are massive and you have no tits!

jokes.text: "She spit in my mouth, Dennis." / "I spit in your mouth after you jammed me in the tit with your scrawny little elbow." / "My elbows are massive and you have no tits!"
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee emerge from the ducts having fought
jokes.punchline: Their mutual complaints escalate from injury to insult — Mac's claim of massive elbows vs. Dee having no tits
jokes.explanation: The escalating mutual insults land well because both Mac's vanity (claiming massive elbows as a point of pride) and Dee's body image being weaponized are deeply character-specific. Mac believing he has massive elbows is a great small absurdist detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis's complete tone shift praising Dee

jokes.text: "I've been warning you about your lack of elbow mass for weeks."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are fighting; Dennis intervenes
jokes.punchline: Dennis, rather than addressing the chaos, calmly references his ongoing concern about Mac's elbow mass as though this is a serious coaching note
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. The absurdity of Dennis having a standing coaching concern about Mac's elbow mass — delivered completely deadpan as a legitimate tactical grievance — is pitch-perfect Dennis character comedy. 'For weeks' implies this is an ongoing conversation Dennis has been having with Mac, which makes it even funnier. It's specific, economical, and deeply character-integrated. Genuinely exceptional line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm trying to get that paper, son

jokes.text: Dennis complimenting Dee with exaggerated sincerity: "You're doing a great job. You are killing it out there, and I'm so proud of you!"
jokes.setup: Dennis just screamed at Mac; now turns to Dee
jokes.punchline: Completely over-the-top sincere praise for Dee, delivered with the same intensity as his insults to Mac — clearly manipulative
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of withering Mac abuse and gushing Dee praise lands because the audience can already sense Dennis is manipulating both. The payoff comes later when his strategy is explained, making this a setup for a bigger joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why do you treat Mac and Dee so differently?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's simple psychology. I withhold compliments from Mac, which makes him angry and subservient. I shower Dee with compliments, which makes her angry at herself.

jokes.text: "Fun Zone dolla dolla bills, y'all" — Dennis presenting laser tag arcade tickets as serious financial currency
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Mac what the point of all this is
jokes.punchline: He pulls out arcade tickets — Fun Zone 'dolla dolla bills' — with complete sincerity, as if these are real money worth grinding for
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating arcade tickets like actual capital is a perfect encapsulation of the episode's core joke — these adults have inverted priorities. 'Dolla dolla bills, y'all' using arcade tickets is funny on its own, and Dennis's complete sincerity elevates it. This line becomes a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'It's another riddle'

jokes.text: Dennis's revealed manipulation strategy: withholding compliments from Mac makes him angry and subservient; showering Dee with compliments makes her feel undeserving and she takes that anger out on children
jokes.setup: Charlie asks why Dennis is managing the group so strangely
jokes.punchline: Dennis has a detailed psychological manipulation system — Mac gets zero compliments to stay angry; Dee gets excessive praise so her self-loathing redirects as aggression onto the kids
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best comedic reveal. It retroactively reframes every Dennis interaction we've seen and makes it funnier. The specificity is what elevates it — not just 'Dennis is manipulative' but *how*: Mac's subservience comes from withholding, Dee's effectiveness comes from exploiting her deep self-loathing and redirecting it at children. 'She takes that anger out on the children' is the punchline and it's dark, specific, and perfectly Dennis. This is Dennis Reynolds at his most distilled. High rewatch value as it recontextualizes earlier scenes.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Pew pew pew pew pew!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Okay. It's another riddle. Let me think on that one, Dennis...'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just explained his complex psychological manipulation system
jokes.punchline: Charlie, unable to process the disturbing truth, files it as a 'riddle' — his coping mechanism for incomprehensibility
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy: one line that (a) characterizes Charlie's limited capacity to process disturbing information, (b) callbacks the riddle running gag, and (c) lets Dennis's manipulation speech land as the actual punchline. 'Let me think on that one' is perfectly Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Is a fart a ghost?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. It's the ghost of lunch

jokes.text: "Okay. Yeah. No, that was a mind-bending riddle. It's a tough one, 'cause you don't think..." — Dennis pivoting to call the blind skydiving joke a riddle after all
jokes.setup: Earlier Dennis called Charlie's blind skydiving thing a joke; Charlie won the argument
jokes.punchline: Dennis quietly capitulates and now calls it a 'mind-bending riddle' — saving face without admitting defeat
jokes.explanation: Dennis's inability to admit defeat is a character staple, and this small capitulation — dressing it up as a 'mind-bending riddle' — works as a quick button on the earlier argument. Not a standout but solid.

dialogue.line: Dennis and Charlie reveal they turn Charlie's pack off so the team doesn't lose points when he gets shot

jokes.text: "Goddamn it, Mac, you thin-elbowed little goblin. You never cease to disappoint me in everything you do."
jokes.setup: Dennis is reverting to his manipulation strategy on Mac
jokes.punchline: "Thin-elbowed little goblin" — the specific, surreal insult calling back to the elbow mass concern and escalating it to a visual slur
jokes.explanation: "Thin-elbowed little goblin" is a genuinely great insult. The specificity of leading with elbows — a body part not typically weaponized in insults — combined with 'goblin' as the final noun makes it both funny and oddly poetic. High quotability, strong callback to the elbow mass running gag. This kind of specific absurd insult is what IASIP does better than almost any other show.

jokes.text: "You really are killing it out there. I'm so proud of you. You're so deserving of my love."
jokes.setup: Dennis's manipulation strategy requires him to shower Dee with compliments
jokes.punchline: "You're so deserving of my love" — delivered to Dee immediately after insulting Mac, now fully revealed as calculated psychological manipulation
jokes.explanation: Now that the manipulation has been explained, hearing Dennis say 'you're so deserving of my love' to Dee is darkly hilarious. The audience knows exactly what's happening and Dee presumably doesn't. 'So deserving of my love' is a strange enough phrase that it lands as both manipulative and weirdly sad given Dee's character.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: an amazing decoy

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: adds a monster element that distracts and frightens but entertains the kids

jokes.text: "Hey, is the answer to your riddle, uh, an ice cube?" "Yeah. Yep, you got it."
jokes.setup: Charlie's earlier riddle about farts/ghosts was left open; Mac has been thinking about it
jokes.punchline: Mac's answer is 'an ice cube' — a completely wrong answer to the blind skydiving riddle; Charlie immediately accepts it as correct
jokes.explanation: Mac's answer of 'ice cube' to the blind skydiving joke makes no sense, and Charlie immediately validates it. This is a great two-character comedy moment — both are equally wrong and both are completely satisfied. The mutual incompetence creates its own closed loop of absurdist logic.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're like Cookie Monster

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Wait, there's no cookies

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Kids are scared of you and not really scared of him

jokes.text: "Is a fart a ghost? ... It's the ghost of lunch."
jokes.setup: Frank appears and Charlie invites him to do riddles; Frank asks if a fart is a ghost
jokes.punchline: "It's the ghost of lunch" — a surprisingly poetic and deeply Frank answer
jokes.explanation: "The ghost of lunch" is a genuinely excellent joke. It has the economy of a perfect punchline, the absurdist poetry of a Frank-and-Charlie bit at its best, and it's immediately quotable. The setup ('is a fart a ghost') is itself funny as a riddle premise, and 'the ghost of lunch' reframes it in a way that's philosophically absurd but also technically kind of correct. This is one of the episode's best lines and a strong candidate for the most quotable. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie happily making laser tag sounds when his pack is turned on for the first time

jokes.text: "Go out to the lobby really quick and get me, like, some chicken wings." "You want hot sauce on 'em?" "No. I forbid it. Absolutely not."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Charlie to do a task while keeping him focused
jokes.punchline: His response to Charlie's offer of hot sauce is 'I forbid it. Absolutely not.' — an absurdly authoritative response to a condiment offer
jokes.explanation: "I forbid it" about hot sauce is a classic Dennis line — treating a minor preference as a matter of authority. The escalation from 'No' to 'I forbid it. Absolutely not.' is good Dennis character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: what Big Mo looks like' is a riddle

jokes.text: "His pack's not even on, for crying out loud." — the reveal that Charlie's laser tag vest has been deactivated
jokes.setup: Charlie has been gleefully running around the laser tag arena making gun sounds
jokes.punchline: His pack has been turned off — he's been making the gun sounds himself and his vest doesn't register hits
jokes.explanation: Strong setup-and-reveal. The audience may have suspected something was off with Charlie's triumphant laser tag report, and this confirms it in the cruelest and funniest way. The reveal lands hard and sets up the even funnier follow-up exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Cantaloupes because if you're holding a pile of cantaloupes, you're not gonna be able to see very much

jokes.text: "But my gun still makes noise." "Well, no... Well, that's you doing that, bud." "No, it isn't." [Charlie tries to make gun noise] "Pew, pe..." "Yeah. See, that's you, bud." "Oh, that is me."
jokes.setup: Charlie is told his pack was turned off and that he was making the gun sounds himself
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists his gun makes noise, tries to demonstrate, makes the pew sound himself, and then accepts the reality with 'Oh, that is me'
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic beats in the episode. The structure is perfect: Charlie's confident denial, the live test where he inadvertently proves it, and the innocent acceptance of 'Oh, that is me.' It's the ideal Charlie moment — dim, childlike, and completely without self-pity. The beat works on multiple levels: the inherent sadness of the revelation, the comedy of his immediate acceptance, and the audience processing both simultaneously. 'Oh, that is me' is an all-time Charlie line. Near the top of the episode's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'You telling me you can see through a pile of cantaloupes?'

jokes.text: "You run around, you're screaming, and you add sort of like a monster element to the game that distracts and frightens but entertains the kids"
jokes.setup: Dennis explains Charlie's 'valuable' role to the team
jokes.punchline: Charlie's role is essentially as a terrifying feral creature who scares children as a distraction — described earnestly as a team contribution
jokes.explanation: Dennis's clinical description of Charlie's 'value' as a child-frightening monster decoy is a great dark joke. The earnestness makes it funnier — Dennis genuinely believes this is a compliment and a valid team role.

dialogue.line: Mac and Dee went to the 'Fun Zone instead of the Maintenance Zone in the ceiling'

jokes.text: "Well, and also the kids are scared of you and they're not really scared of him." — explaining why Charlie is not like the Cookie Monster
jokes.setup: Mac has compared Charlie to Cookie Monster to soften the monster revelation
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects the comparison: Cookie Monster isn't scary, Charlie is actually frightening to children
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean button on the Cookie Monster bit. The implication that Charlie actually terrorizes children in the arena is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's not a joke, that's a riddle. And don't steal my shit, you stupid bird-faced bitch!

jokes.text: "Oh. Oh, that makes some good sounds." — Charlie's delighted reaction to his now-activated pack making real beeping sounds
jokes.setup: Charlie's pack has just been turned on, he expected nothing
jokes.punchline: Charlie is immediately delighted by the sounds his pack makes — real electronic sounds, not his mouth sounds — as if this is a completely new experience
jokes.explanation: This is a lovely payoff to the pew-pew revelation. Charlie's innocent wonder at the pack's sounds — having been making them himself this whole time — is both funny and weirdly touching. His contentment is very Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: 'Rutherford B. Crazy, of course' when asked about the $100 bill

jokes.text: "It's cool, right?" "That's really cool." — Dennis and Mac admiring the pack sounds with Charlie
jokes.setup: Charlie is delighted by his pack's sounds after being previously deceived
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac respond with genuine-seeming agreement, though they were the ones who had it turned off
jokes.explanation: Brief moment, works as a beat. The guilt-tinged 'that's really cool' from the guys who betrayed Charlie is a soft joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Rutherford B. Crazy started in the laser beam business and never gave up on the fundamentals

jokes.text: "That's not cool, man." "Shut up, man. Just... shut up. He just believed it. It's... you know, it's not cool." "It's pretty cool."
jokes.setup: Charlie has left happy; Mac and Dennis quietly discuss
jokes.punchline: The brief argument about whether deceiving Charlie is 'cool' — Mac defending it, with quiet resignation — before they settle on 'it's pretty cool'
jokes.explanation: "It's pretty cool" as the final word on exploiting Charlie's trust is a great cringe beat. Mac's flicker of conscience gives way immediately. This is very IASIP — the momentary awareness of being terrible, quickly embraced. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis's motivational speech about Rutherford's laser beam business

jokes.text: "Some fat little brat, probably." — Dennis's guess at what Big Mo looks like
jokes.setup: Charlie asks what Dennis thinks Big Mo looks like
jokes.punchline: Without hesitation: "Some fat little brat, probably"
jokes.explanation: Quick character comedy — Dennis's instant contempt for a child he's never met is very him. The delivery likely sells this more than the line itself.

dialogue.speaker: Mac and Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't think Rutherford be a real person. That's a cartoon.

jokes.text: "Oh. Oh, is that a riddle? What the kid looks like. Is it, is it a riddle?"
jokes.setup: Dennis describes Big Mo as a fat little brat
jokes.punchline: Charlie thinks Dennis is posing a riddle — unable to distinguish between a descriptive statement and a puzzle
jokes.explanation: Callback to the riddle theme — Charlie now seeing everything as a potential riddle. His inability to distinguish categories of speech is good ongoing character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: created a diversion by telling one dad another dad said his kid had a 'tight little dumper'

jokes.text: "The more you have of it, the less you see." Charlie's answer: "Cantaloupes." "...because if you're holding a pile of cantaloupes, you're not gonna be able to see very much. Especially if it goes past your face."
jokes.setup: Dennis poses the classic 'darkness' riddle
jokes.punchline: Charlie answers 'cantaloupes' with a fully developed logical explanation involving how a pile of cantaloupes obstructs vision
jokes.explanation: One of the all-time great Charlie moments. The answer 'cantaloupes' to 'the more you have of it, the less you see' is already funny, but Charlie's confident defense of his answer — that a large enough pile of cantaloupes would indeed obstruct vision, 'especially if it goes past your face' — takes it to another level entirely. The logic is unassailable on its own terms. This is Charlie's best joke in the episode and a perfect encapsulation of his character: not stupid so much as operating on a completely different plane of reasoning. 'Especially if it goes past your face' is the perfect button. Exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank went to 'Wing Zone' instead of 'war zone' because of the line

jokes.text: "Yeah, but how are you gonna hold a pile of darkness? Does that..."
jokes.setup: Dennis reveals the answer to the riddle is 'darkness'
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately finds a logical flaw in 'darkness' — you can't hold it — implying his cantaloupes answer is MORE practical
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the cantaloupe bit. Charlie turns the tables on Dennis's 'correct' answer by pointing out its physical impracticality — you can't hold darkness, but you CAN hold cantaloupes. His wrong answer is now more defensible than the right one. This escalation of Charlie's logic is the funniest moment in the riddle sequence and one of the best in the episode.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God. That's such a great joke. I would never... How do you even come up with this stuff? You're so worthy of my laughter. You're so worthy."
jokes.setup: Dee makes a mild joke about the 'Maintenance Zone'; Dennis pivots immediately to praising her
jokes.punchline: "You're so worthy of my laughter. You're so worthy." — Dennis's manipulation praise reaching absurd new heights
jokes.explanation: "You're so worthy of my laughter" is a strange, slightly off-human phrase that makes it funnier — it doesn't quite sound like a real compliment, which makes Dennis's manipulation both obvious and disturbing. Good running gag payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis explaining Charlie will lose his 'little plastic army guys' and 'box of bouncy balls' if they stop winning

jokes.text: "She told the lamest joke earlier about a blind guy and a dog or some shit..." "Yeah." "Hey! That's not a joke, that's a riddle!"
jokes.setup: Mac tries to insult Dee by referencing her earlier blind/dog joke
jokes.punchline: Charlie defends the honor of his riddle — angrily insisting it's not a joke, it's a riddle — having completely forgotten his own ambivalence about its status earlier
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Charlie has now fully committed to the riddle classification he was uncertain about earlier. The indignation is funny and consistent with how Charlie defends things he cares about.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I eat bouncy balls to 'test them in my stomach to see how they pass'

jokes.text: "Don't steal my shit, you stupid bird-faced bitch! I'll blast you to pieces!"
jokes.setup: Charlie defending his riddle from being attributed to Dee
jokes.punchline: Charlie escalates from 'don't steal my shit' to threatening to blast Dee to pieces — over credit for the blind skydiving riddle
jokes.explanation: The escalation from intellectual property dispute to laser tag threats is funny. 'Bird-faced bitch' is standard IASIP Dee abuse; it works in context but isn't fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: a ghost, like the fart of meals past

jokes.text: "Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. Now we're jamming. Now we're jamming." — Dennis, satisfied that his manipulation has reignited aggression
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are shouting insults and threats at Dee
jokes.punchline: Dennis watches the chaos he engineered with the satisfied tone of a conductor whose orchestra is playing well
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-satisfied 'now we're jamming' is a great character beat — he engineered this chaos deliberately and is proud of it. Good payoff to the manipulation reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Rutherford B. Crazy's real name was Larry Takashi and he worked with him in the '90s

jokes.text: "Rutherford B. Crazy, of course." — Mac's confident answer to whose face is on the $100 bill
jokes.setup: Dennis asks whose face is on the 100 dollar bill as a rhetorical setup for a motivational speech
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently and incorrectly answers 'Rutherford B. Crazy'
jokes.explanation: "Rutherford B. Crazy, of course" is an exceptional joke. The 'of course' sells it — Mac is not guessing, he is completely certain. The name itself (Rutherford B. Crazy — a parody of presidential naming conventions, B. for 'Be') is brilliant. And crucially, Dennis doesn't correct him, which is its own joke. This is one of the most quotable lines in the episode and a perfect Mac stupidity moment. High marks for originality and economy.

dialogue.line: Larry Takashi threw himself down a wishing well with suicide note saying 'It all meant nothing'

jokes.text: "He get to go out and be whatever the hell he want to be. He get to be crazy." — Dennis's motivational speech about the laser tag mascot's work ethic
jokes.setup: Dennis is using the fictional laser tag mascot as an inspirational figure
jokes.punchline: The philosophical payoff is that after grinding, you get to 'be crazy' — which means being a cartoon character on laser tag tickets
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating the cartoon mascot's lifestyle as an aspirational model is funny, especially since he's delivering this as a genuine motivational speech. The arc from 'he had a dream' to 'he get to be crazy' is nicely absurd.

dialogue.line: We ain't going anywhere. We're never leaving, you little piece of shit.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I don't think Rutherford be a real person. That's a cartoon.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is delivering his inspirational Rutherford B. Crazy speech with total confidence
jokes.punchline: Mac and Frank casually inform Dennis that Rutherford B. Crazy is a cartoon mascot, not a real person — the entire motivational framework collapses
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom deflation: an inspiring speech built on false premises. The nonchalance of 'that's a cartoon' as the speech-ender is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You thought we'd gone? We ain't going anywhere

jokes.text: "Uh, I don't think Rutherford be a real person. That's a cartoon."
jokes.setup: Dennis has been delivering a full motivational speech about Rutherford B. Crazy as if he's a real historical figure
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie point out he's a cartoon, completely deflating the speech
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Dennis's motivational speech by the revelation that his inspirational figure is a cartoon character is well-timed and funny. The calm delivery makes it better.

jokes.text: "Death is gonna come in the form of a fat child, who will turn us into a fart. It sounds crazy now that I'm saying it. Dennis explained it a lot more better."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee ask why they can't go have fun; Charlie relays Dennis's warning
jokes.punchline: Charlie's summary of Dennis's speech — death as a fat child turning them into farts — sounds absurd even to Charlie, who adds 'Dennis explained it a lot more better'
jokes.explanation: "A lot more better" is perfect Charlie grammar, and his summary of Dennis's speech is a great comedic reduction — the entire philosophical argument reduced to 'fat child turns us into fart.' The self-awareness that it 'sounds crazy' is unusual for Charlie and that meta-flicker makes it funnier. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: "I told this one dad that another dad said that his kid had a tight little dumper."
jokes.setup: Frank explains the diversion he created — Charlie asks what happened
jokes.punchline: Frank's diversion tactic was telling one dad that another dad made a lewd comment about his child — causing a brawl
jokes.explanation: Very Frank — using deliberately inflammatory information about children to cause a physical fight as a laser tag diversion. The specificity of 'tight little dumper' is both disgusting and funny. Frank's casual delivery of this as a tactical success is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: "A war zone? I was in the Wing Zone. You know, it was such a line. I mean, I had to create a melee to disperse it."
jokes.setup: Dennis says Mac and Dee are getting slaughtered in the 'war zone'
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies he was in the Wing Zone (the chicken wing section), and had to create a physical fight to get through the line
jokes.explanation: War Zone / Wing Zone wordplay works well and reveals Frank's entirely self-serving mission. His solution to a long line — creating a physical melee — is perfectly Frank. Good economy in the delivery.

jokes.text: "Oh, shit, did you get hit? Did you get hit?" "Oh. No, no, no, no. No, Charlie. That's my signal that the food is ready."
jokes.setup: Frank's vest beeps; Charlie thinks he's been hit in laser tag
jokes.punchline: It's the food buzzer signaling his wings are ready — Frank has a restaurant pager on while playing laser tag
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection beat. The reveal that Frank's signal is the food buzzer, not a laser hit, is a satisfying twist that also characterizes Frank perfectly — he's playing laser tag while monitoring his food order.

jokes.text: Charlie activating his pack and making the sound effect with his mouth as Frank leaves — "See how happy he was? I made a sound, too, 'cause I feel like that was..."
jokes.setup: Frank's vest beeped; Charlie activates his own pack to 'match' Frank's excitement
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains he made a mouth sound too in solidarity — the pew-pew habit persists even now that his pack works
jokes.explanation: Sweet callback — Charlie still makes mouth sounds by habit/solidarity even with a working pack. This is a lovely character detail.

jokes.text: "You are messing it up. You are messing it all up!"
jokes.setup: Charlie joined in with Frank's food buzzer moment enthusiastically
jokes.punchline: Dennis erupts at Charlie for 'messing it all up' — the grand strategy apparently derailed by a pack beep and Charlie's happiness
jokes.explanation: Standard Dennis frustration beat. Works in context but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: "What, obesity?" — Charlie's guess at what Big Mo represents
jokes.setup: Dennis says Big Mo isn't really about the kid, it's about what he represents
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately guesses 'obesity'
jokes.explanation: Perfect one-word punchline with maximum economy. 'Obesity' as a callback to their earlier discussion about kids being fat, now promoted to existential symbol, is a great comedic payoff. The delivery — casual, matter-of-fact — makes it land even harder. Genuinely excellent joke.

jokes.text: "No! Not obesity. I don't even know if the kid's fat. He's just called..." "He's probably fat." "He's probably fat." "Yeah. Obesity rates being what they are, he's a fat kid."
jokes.setup: Dennis denies Big Mo represents obesity
jokes.punchline: All three immediately agree the kid is definitely fat based on obesity statistics, completely derailing Dennis's philosophical point
jokes.explanation: The group consensus that this unknown child is definitely fat — supported by citing childhood obesity statistics — is a great tangent that derails Dennis's serious moment. The deadpan 'obesity rates being what they are' as a statistical argument is very good.

jokes.text: "Feel like all those kids are fat." "They eat so much sugar these days, man." "Well, it's in everything."
jokes.setup: The group has gone off-track discussing childhood obesity
jokes.punchline: All three engage in a brief, earnest conversation about sugar content in food — these are grown men who play laser tag for arcade tickets having a public health discussion
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of this gang having a mundane nutritional discussion mid-game is funny but mostly works as texture. Not a standout.

jokes.text: "Like the fart of meals past? You just dissipate into the air, and then everybody forgets that you ever smelled up the place?"
jokes.setup: Dennis is warning Charlie about legacy and obscurity if they quit
jokes.punchline: His metaphor for obscurity is becoming 'the fart of meals past' — a callback to Frank's ghost-of-lunch riddle, now used as an existential threat
jokes.explanation: "The fart of meals past" is a great phrase that callbacks to Frank's 'ghost of lunch' riddle and extends it into philosophy. Dennis using a fart metaphor for existential oblivion is both funny and strangely poetic. It also foreshadows the Rutherford B. Crazy suicide reveal thematically.

jokes.text: "Did you see the look on that kid's face when I grabbed his glasses and I threw 'em on the ground and stomped all over 'em?" "He blasted us to pieces, but it was worth it just to see his little ass cry."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee come back excited from playing in the game
jokes.punchline: Their highlight is physically destroying a child's glasses and making him cry — described with evident joy
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP dark comedy — adults enthusiastically terrorizing children in pursuit of fun. 'It was worth it just to see his little ass cry' is a perfect punchline that encapsulates how terrible these people are while being genuinely funny. The score tradeoff (got blasted to pieces but destroyed a child's eyewear) is a good comedic structure.

jokes.text: Larry Takashi (Rutherford B. Crazy) drove himself to a wishing well and threw himself into it
jokes.setup: Frank reveals the founder of Laser Tag Fun Zone killed himself
jokes.punchline: His suicide method: driving to a wishing well and throwing himself down it — an absurdly whimsical way to die
jokes.explanation: "Drove himself to a wishing well and threw himself down it" is a masterfully absurd detail. The specificity of a wishing well for a suicide — a place associated with hope and wishes — applied to a laser tag mogul creates a darkly comic image. It's funny and bleak simultaneously, which is IASIP at its best. High originality.

jokes.text: "He wrote a suicide note on a Fun Zone dolla dolla bill, and it said, 'It all meant nothing.'"
jokes.setup: Frank relays the details of Rutherford B. Crazy's suicide
jokes.punchline: The suicide note was written on a Fun Zone arcade ticket — the dolla dolla bill that Dennis has been chasing all episode — with the message 'It all meant nothing'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of the strongest moments in the episode overall. The suicide note written on a Fun Zone dolla dolla bill saying 'It all meant nothing' perfectly closes the dolla dolla bills running gag, punctuates the episode's thematic argument about meaningless grind, and is genuinely dark and funny simultaneously. The specificity of the medium (arcade ticket) and the message ('It all meant nothing') creates a moment of comedy and pathos that's earned. It recontextualizes everything Dennis has been doing all episode. Exceptional craft — this is why the episode works.

jokes.text: "Nobody came to his funeral. According to this, his employees all hated him, and his family barely knew him."
jokes.setup: The group is processing Rutherford B. Crazy's death
jokes.punchline: The portrait of a successful businessman who died completely alone — a dark mirror for the gang's own relationships
jokes.explanation: More thematic than comedic, but the bleak portrait of Larry Takashi functions as a joke through its implicit comparison to the gang. The deadpan delivery of a succession of tragedies ('nobody came to his funeral') works as dark comedy.

jokes.text: "Shit. So Rutherford be rich. Rutherford be successful as all hell. But you know what else Rutherford be? Rutherford be right."
jokes.setup: Dennis processes the story of Larry Takashi's miserable success
jokes.punchline: He delivers the eulogy/lesson using the 'Rutherford be X' construction from earlier — 'Rutherford be right' — the structure now turned into philosophical wisdom
jokes.explanation: "Rutherford be right" is a great payoff to the Rutherford B. Crazy running gag. The linguistic construction ('he be X') has been a running joke, and now it's redeployed as genuine emotional beat. The structure is excellent — it's both funny and genuinely affecting. Dennis's moment of self-awareness is rare and the callback makes it land harder.

jokes.text: "Goodbye, base?" "Goodbye to the base we've held down for so long."
jokes.setup: The gang decides to leave the base and end their laser tag ritual
jokes.punchline: The solemn farewell to a laser tag base — delivered with the gravity of people leaving a home or ending a chapter of life
jokes.explanation: The earnest ceremony of leaving a laser tag base they've defended 'for so long' is funny and strangely moving. The gap between the gravity of their emotion and the triviality of the subject is the joke.

jokes.text: "I am gonna miss it. But it's time to let Big Mo have it."
jokes.setup: The gang is saying goodbye to their laser tag base
jokes.punchline: Dennis says this with complete sincerity — he will genuinely miss a laser tag base; and 'letting Big Mo have it' is delivered as an act of magnanimous sacrifice
jokes.explanation: The solemnity with which Dennis speaks about Big Mo inheriting the laser tag base is funny in context. It's the irony of adults treating this as deeply meaningful.

jokes.text: "Hey, Big Mo." — the gang has returned to the base and is confronting Big Mo
jokes.setup: The gang decided to let Big Mo have the base and move on — a whole philosophical arc
jokes.punchline: They're back. They haven't left. The entire philosophical journey was for nothing — they never moved.
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode. The entire philosophical arc — Rutherford, fart ghosts, dolla dolla bills, Larry Takashi's suicide, the solemn goodbye — all of it, and they just... came back. 'Hey, Big Mo' delivered after all that soul-searching is the perfect Always Sunny ending. It's the show's thesis in a single scene: these people are incapable of change. The misdirection is total — the audience was led to believe they were actually going to evolve — and the reversal is both funny and thematically resonant. The structure is excellent.

jokes.text: "Oh, what? You thought we'd gone? You'd like that, wouldn't you? We ain't going anywhere. We're never leaving, you little piece of shit."
jokes.setup: Big Mo arrives at the base expecting it to be abandoned
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a villain monologue to what is presumably a child — 'you little piece of shit' — with absolute menace about never leaving
jokes.explanation: "We ain't going anywhere. We're never leaving, you little piece of shit" to a child is a great IASIP ending. All the philosophical growth, all the Larry Takashi lessons — abandoned in favor of threatening a child at a laser tag base. It's deeply character-integrated for Dennis and closes the episode beautifully. 'Let him have it' (the subsequent laser barrage) is the perfect button.

jokes.text: "Yeah, light him up." — the gang opens fire on Big Mo
jokes.setup: Dennis tells the gang to let Big Mo have it
jokes.punchline: The gang blasts Big Mo — a child — with everything they have, the final image of the episode
jokes.explanation: The final button — 'Yeah, light him up' as the gang unleashes on Big Mo after all their philosophical hand-wringing — is a perfect closing gag. The pivot from 'it all meant nothing, let's enjoy life' to 'destroy this child' is the show's comedic ethos in one scene. Great economy in the line delivery.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, light him up.' — The gang opens fire on Big Mo
jokes.setup: Dennis has just told Big Mo they're never leaving
jokes.punchline: 'Light him up' — the gang commits to destroying a child in laser tag with the intensity of a military operation
jokes.explanation: 'Yeah, light him up' as the button on the whole episode — anti-climactic in the best way, and exactly the right register of casual brutality toward a child's laser tag experience. Perfect economy for a final joke.

tmdb_overview: In this spoof of Waiting for Godot, Dennis and Charlie stand guard at their laser tag base waiting to ambush their enemy, Big Mo, but Dennis has doubts about why they play laser tag and whether or not the victory is worth it.
